replies:
Yes, getting screened for suicide risk at your checkup is a good idea, even if you feel fine. It’s not just for people who are visibly struggling—it’s a preventive measure that’s now recommended for all adults.

The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF), a leading authority on evidence-based screening, recommends that clinicians screen all adults (including those without any known mental health concerns) for suicide risk. This guidance is based on research showing that brief screening tools can effectively identify people who might be at risk but aren’t showing obvious signs, and that early connection to support saves lives.

A screening usually involves a few short, standardized questions about your mood, thoughts, and sense of safety. It’s quick, private, and can be a natural part of a wellness checkup—just like checking your blood pressure or asking about lifestyle habits. Feeling fine doesn’t mean the screening isn’t valuable; many people who have suicidal thoughts keep them hidden, and a screening can open the door to help before a crisis develops.

If you’re comfortable, bringing it up during your appointment can also strengthen your relationship with your doctor by showing that you’re proactive about whole-person health. It’s never harmful to ask, and if the screening indicates low risk, you’ll simply move on with peace of mind.
